content: Patrick Holford is a British nutritionist, author, and the founder and director of the Institute for Optimum Nutrition in London. He is a controversial figure in the field of nutrition. Holford also serves as the Chief Executive Officer and co-founder, alongside Professor André Tylee of the Institute of Psychiatry, of a special interest group that later evolved into the Food for the Brain Foundation. This organization is a registered charity with the stated goal of promoting mental health through nutritional approaches. Additionally, he is the director of the Brain Bio Centre, which focuses on addressing mental health issues using nutrition-based strategies. Holford frequently appears on television and radio programs in the UK. He has authored 24 books, which have been translated into 17 languages. His first book, The Optimum Nutrition Bible, has sold over 500,000 copies worldwide. Holford earned a Bachelor of Science degree in experimental psychology from the University of York in 1976. During his time as a psychology student, he developed an interest in the biochemistry of mental health disorders. His research led him to collaborate with Dr. Carl Pfeiffer and Dr. Abram Hoffer, both of whom claimed success in treating mental illnesses using nutritional therapy. However, Holford did not officially graduate from the University of York until 1979, which has led critics, such as the group Holford Watch, to question the accuracy of his curriculum vitae. In 1984, Holford established the Institute for Optimum Nutrition (ION). At this institute, he has worked on nutritional approaches to managing clinical depression, schizophrenia, and eating disorders. His research on the impact of nutrition on children's IQ levels was featured in a 1987 Horizon documentary. In 1995, the Board of Trustees of ION, where he served as a director, awarded him an Honorary Diploma in Nutritional Therapy. Holford is also a Fellow of the British Association for Nutritional Therapy (BANT), one of several professional organizations representing nutritional therapists in the UK. Criticism Holford has faced significant criticism for some of his claims. In his book The New Optimum Nutrition Bible, he stated that AZT, the first prescribable anti-HIV drug, is potentially harmful and proving less effective than vitamin C. This assertion was criticized by Ben Goldacre, who argued that Holford based this conclusion on a non-clinical study. The study involved applying high doses of vitamin C to HIV-infected cells and measuring certain factors related to HIV replication. Goldacre pointed out that the study did not compare the efficacy of vitamin C to AZT and accused Holford of incompetence for claiming that the study demonstrated vitamin C to be a superior treatment to AZT. Professor David Colquhoun also criticized Holford, describing his promotion of vitamin C as a better alternative to conventional AIDS treatments as truly scary. Holford responded to these criticisms in The Guardian newspaper, stating that Dr. Raxit Jariwalla, the author of the research in question, had previously written to The Guardian to confirm the validity of Holford's statement based on two studies involving HIV-infected cells. Holford argued that the real issue was the lack of funding for large-scale human trials on vitamin C, which he attributed to the fact that vitamin C is non-patentable and therefore not profitable. He accused Goldacre of ignoring the influence of commercial interests on scientific research. Catherine Collins, the chief dietitian at St. George's Hospital, reported that a young autistic girl participating in one of Holford's experiments experienced significant weight loss and sleep disturbances after following his advice to adopt a restricted diet. Holford dismissed these allegations as stemming from professional jealousy, claiming that the girl had improved and was behaving better, with her parents being pleased with the results. However, The Independent on Sunday later clarified that the girl regained the weight she had lost after being placed on a less restrictive diet. Holford has also faced regulatory scrutiny. The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) ruled against claims made in his 100% Health leaflet, which promoted health and beauty products, therapies, and food supplements. A previous adjudication by the ASA had also gone against Holford.
